Study example: linguistic complexity in presidential speeches

NOTE: The optional “A closer look” boxes suggest ways to develop this simple study further. You can follow the worked example without opening them; their exercises are suggestions, not additional steps used in the run described here.

The question and prompt

Have American presidents become more plainly spoken over time, as is often said? Do more recent presidents use simpler words and shorter sentences even on formal occasions? In this mini-study, we will try to get at an answer to these questions by examining a central genre of presidential speech – the inaugural address – over time (the 60-speech corpus is available for download under “Corpus examples”). A very simple prompt to examine the linguistic complexity of these speeches could look like this:

“Rate the linguistic complexity of this US presidential inaugural address on a 1–7 scale — considering vocabulary, sentence structure, and register together, as a reader would experience them — from 1 (plain, direct, accessible language) to 7 (formal, dense, demanding language).

Give:

1. Score (1–7)

2. One representative sentence illustrating that level”

The score gives a numerical rating we can analyze. The quote gives us a sense of what that rating might be capturing.

Running the annotation

I started by adding my OpenAI API key to the project (1), which allows the project to spend my prepaid funds. I added the annotation prompt and selected the model (gpt-5.6-luna) and reasoning effort (medium) (2). I added the presidential speech corpus by dragging the corpus files into the upload window (3). After trying on a few texts, I ran the annotation (“Run all”), which completed in a few minutes, and downloaded the results as an Excel file (4).

NOTE: Annotating all 60 speeches with GPT-6 Luna, a newer model, at medium reasoning effort costs about 2 cents and takes just under a minute. With the more powerful GPT-6.1 Sol, the cost is about 50 cents.

Interpreting the results

Here is the distribution of scores over time (produced by uploading the Excel file to Claude and asking for a graph displaying change over time):

What jumps out at you? At least three results seem immediately noteworthy:

First, there seems to be something to it: although there are outliers, the trendline suggests that at least this genre of presidential speech has become less linguistically complex and demanding over time. This exercise can’t tell us why, although it may provide hints. But it is a nice bit of support for the received view.

Second, note the extremely high linguistic complexity of speeches by early presidents. This is not at all a novel finding, but it’s still striking to see it laid out like this. Here’s a taste, in the form of the very first sentence of John Adams’s first inaugural address (March 4, 1797):

“When it was first perceived, in early times, that no middle course for America remained between unlimited submission to a foreign legislature and a total independence of its claims, men of reflection were less apprehensive of danger from the formidable power of fleets and armies they must determine to resist than from those contests and dissensions which would certainly arise concerning the forms of government to be instituted over the whole and over the parts of this extensive country.”

Third, two of the lowest scores are very recent. They belong to the current president: Donald J. Trump. Officially, the first sentence of his second inaugural address (January 20, 2025) is “Thank you.” The first real statement is “the golden age of America begins right now.”

But there’s another “3” in the sample. That’s Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s fourth (!) inaugural address (January 20, 1945). Did FDR talk like Trump? More precisely – because it’s easy to be glib about results like this – did FDR use language comparable in complexity to that of Donald Trump, or at least his speechwriter?

No: his previous three speeches are more linguistically complex. What’s going on?

FDR was at this point gravely ill, and visibly failing. He’d be dead within three months. It’s not surprising that he toned it down on this occasion. Also, the U.S. was fighting a two-front war, and an elaborate performance might have been perceived as tone-deaf against the background of wartime austerity (the whole ceremony was scaled down). Finally, it was his fourth inauguration, so people basically knew what he was about. There was less of a need to present his political vision in argumentative and rhetorical fullness. For these reasons, it’s perhaps not surprising that this was the very first sentence of the address:

“Mr. Chief Justice, Mr. Vice President, my friends, you will understand and, I believe, agree with my wish that the form of this inauguration be simple and its words brief.”

So, it makes sense!

The results of this exercise not only tell us something general about the complexity of the speeches over time; they also indicate which specific speeches might be especially interesting to look at in a closer analysis, as with FDR’s fourth inaugural address. You can fruitfully combine the general, high-level results of an annotation batch like this with a more selective and interpretive approach.

Checking the results

That’s not to say you can always trust an annotation result to be correct or insightful. The results can be misleading or even outright false. They can be made so, for example, by the researcher’s own confusions, poor prompt design, or the use of an insufficiently powerful model. The results are not self-interpreting, and they should definitely not be trusted blindly. It is good practice to check results against independent human ratings of a varied sample of speeches and investigate disagreements. You can also ask the model for a brief justification and supporting passages, then check whether these support its judgment.

That’s it for this little illustration. For more information about conducting a real, full-scale study using LLM-based text annotation, see the practical guidelines and methodological papers referenced under “Further resources.”
